newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - Action after pullback key to U.S. stocks.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - Action after pullback key to U.S. stocks.

text.p: Wall Street stocks' ability to rally to fresh highs after their current pullback will be a key indicator of the bull market's health.

Technical analysts agreed that last week's downturn in the Dow Industrial Average on record New York Stock Exchange volume signalled a break in the uptrend that began in mid-December. Several analysts see a pullback to around 6500.
The true test of the major bull trend will come when stocks attempt to rally again, they said.
If, after a period that could last several months, the stocks do not have enough power to break to new highs, then falter anew, a bearish "topping" process could set in, technical analysts said.
"You can't call (the current action on Wall Street) anything other than a short-term correction/consolidation until you get a topping process," said Jonathan Dodd, technical analyst at Dean Witter.
The Dow was off 37 points at 6659 in afternoon trading after shedding 137 points last week.
The near-term turning point came last Thursday after the Dow hit an intraday peak of 6907, then reversed ground to end off 94 points on record single-day volume.
NYSE volume last week was its biggest ever at 2.82 billion shares, eclipsing the record set the week ended January 10, which had 2.72 billion.
Joseph Barthel, director of investment strategy at Fahnestock, said volume tends to peak at least three months, and up to nine months, before a bull-market peak in the Dow.
"On an intermediate-term basis the expansive volume was very constructive," Barthel said.
He said he expected the Dow to establish a broad trading range -- between about 6500 and 7000 -- over the next several months during which leadership will switch to small stocks from large ones.

Barthel said charts comparing the relative performance of the Russell 2000 index, a barometer of small-capitalization stocks, with the Standard & Poor's 500 imply that "we're in the very early stages of outperformance of the Russell 2000."

Alan Newman, technical analyst at H.D. Brous & Co, said he was expecting a topping pattern to emerge, with U.S. stocks failing to rally above their previous highs after what he said he expects to be a 10 percent correction.

"This time around they're not going to make new highs," Newman said. "They'll take the market back maybe half way. Then we'll have another 10 percent decline. I think at that point we'll see buyers again but by that time it will be too late, we'll be in a bear market."

Newman said he expected the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates at its February 4-5 policy-making meeting. Also sapping the market's strength is the narrowing breadth as measured by the advance-decline lines on both the NYSE and the Nasdaq, he said.
